> How does IsExtensionData work? 

There can be at most one properties marked ExtensionData per type. On serialization it will serialize key/value pairs as inlined properties of the underlying JSON object and conversely, it will be populated with deserialized properties not matching with any of the other properties. See also https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.text.json.serialization.jsonextensiondataattribute?view=net-6.0#remarks
Closing in favor of #63686, I moved part of the checklist to the "Progress" section there for more visibility.

review_comments: I'll recommend that we also lock options instance here
See https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/71797#discussion_r916741046
do we need to rename this in every PR?
Mea culpa. In this case I renamed these for consistency with the newly added `GetTypeInfo` method.

since you're effectively doing almost everything from scratch it probably makes sense to also do JsonTypeInfo from scratch and implement it as IJsonTypeInfoResolver which returns null for types it can't handle and on the usage site combine that with DefaultJsonTypeInfoResolver
Maybe we can look at that in the next round of functional tests. I wanted to refactor that as soon as `Order` got implemented.
file an issue with any remaining work

I get that extending this pattern to other functional tests would be nice to have, but honestly don't see why we need to do this now? Do you have concerns about test coverage? Would you like to maybe contribute another PR that adds additional function tests? We have a checkmark for that in #71797.
protected members should follow naming convention for public members (`List`)
We use naming conventions for member types and not accessibility modifiers. This is the appropriate naming convention for a field.
you might want to test scenario where this is called from resolver and causing some recursion to happen

Added, although it's simply validating that a resolver calling back into `options.GetTypeInfo` will prompt a stack overflow. This is fine, similar behaviors arise in improper uses of `option.GetConverter` as well.
do we need reverse test? changing one extension data into the other property? Also I'm missing functional test where user incorrectly set two extension data properties and we fix that

See https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/71797#discussion_r916751712. Having two attributes will currently fail early. I will add a test that causes `Configure` to fail if the resolver specifies duplicate properties with `IsExtensionData`.

the only reason we wanted IsExtensionData over single nullable ExtensionDataProperty is so that user can fix errors with attributes and seems we can't do that which kinda kills the purpose of that. We should validate this is viable in this PR
Done.

> the only reason we wanted IsExtensionData over single nullable ExtensionDataProperty is so that user can fix errors with attributes and seems we can't do that which kinda kills the purpose of that. We should validate this is viable in this PR

I agree, and we should strive to fix this in the future. We can change behaviors that throw exceptions but we cannot change bad APIs being shipped.
should we do something with the result?
Don't care enough I think, just needed to make sure the metadata can be used both ways without error. We have other tests validating functional correctness for this overload.

so if user incorrectly places the attribute on something which is not meant to be extension data it's impossible to correct that error? should we be doing validation in the configure to allow to fix the incorrect user setting?

I settled for throwing behavior right now because pushing it to `Configure` necessitated substantial refactoring of the `CacheMember` logic. I attempted doing that but ended up breaking a bunch of member visibility tests in subtle ways.  We can revisit the behavior and move all validation to `Configure` in vNext (at the same time we fix all the `JsonIgnoreAttribute` bugs)

FWIW we currently also throw early when we encounter other invalid configuration, e.g. when we have conflicting property names.
Why substantial refactoring? we only need to not throw on IsExtensionData and just set it to true based on attribute presence. We move throwing into configure (IsExtensionData + invalid type)

It's not just validating that the type is right, there's also the concern of validating duplicate annotations. In order to make this possible, we need to stop building the property cache early in the case of reflection metadata. But, like I said this requires refactoring of the member resolution which I attempted. We need to do this eventually, but it should not regress member visibility behavior and it should not regress performance in the default use (i.e. reflection-based metadata without custom resolvers should not necessitate building the property cache twice).
you might want to add assert which checks that what you assigned is what you get
Sure.
I'm missing also test where class has no extension data properties and we incorrectly modify contract to make 2 or more
Yup, will address in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/71797#discussion_r916752391
please file an issue on any gaps if we're not planning to fix it now
It's been already addressed, I'm saying it's the same concern as the one raised in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/71797#discussion_r916752391.
ditto
I don't think we should be pre-sorting anymore

I was having similar thoughts, but ultimately decided against it for a few reasons:

1. The source generator already pre-sorts properties at compile-time.
2. The reflection resolver must precompute the property cache at construction time (it's needed when walking the type hierarchy). For performance reasons it only gets invalidated if the user explicitly requires the public property list. If the original property order were preserved it would necessitate duplicating some of the cache calculations at the `Configure` stage regardless of whether properties are being customized.
3. The order of reflection-based member enumeration can be nondeterministic depending on the runtime.

1. that is a simple fix, not really an argument
2. it does not. It can move its logic to LateAdd and do exactly the same as source gen does
3. how do you know it's not deterministic? - regardless it's still not deterministic with pre-sorting by order

> that is a simple fix, not really an argument

What? Why would we want to _regress_ source generator performance and force sorting at runtime?

> It can move its logic to LateAdd and do exactly the same as source gen does

Perhaps, that would require another round of refactoring though.

> how do you know it's not deterministic?

See https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/2330#issuecomment-597326402, https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/46272. It will be fixed in CLR for .NET 7 but since we're supporting other runtimes as well, for all intents and purposes the order of members is nondeterministic.

> Why would we want to regress source generator performance and force sorting at runtime?

we can leave source gen as is but not pre-sort for reflection. source gen is separate resolver and can have different defaults than reflection

> for all intents and purposes the order of members is nondeterministic.

perhaps runtime is non-deterministic but we can be deterministic w.r.t to runtime and use runtime provided order
For reasons already stated I strongly disagree. I'm not making that change.
we could loop here and test couple of other classes as well since json name matches property name
Not sure I follow?
also type could be an argument to a theory and we can check that for multiple types
What specific functionality do you feel is not being covered by the existing test?

I'm wondering if we should return null instead, that would match IJsonTypeInfoResolver. Also I just noticed that our docs for GetConverter claim we return null when there is no converter but they also claim we throw - we might want to match behavior and fix docs so it's clear if we return null or throw:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.text.json.jsonserializeroptions.getconverter?view=net-6.0
I think we should make the docs match with the shipped behavior.
either way is fine but we should be consistent at least
Sure, but this is not related to the scope of this change in the slightest way possible.
honestly I think it would be ok if we locked options when it's called

After further investigations, I have concluded that generating metadata with mutable options does not actually compromise the cache. Plus, this makes semantics consistent with how `GetConverter` behaves.
